senses.gloss:
sabhāpati
(‘president of a meeting’)
------------------------------------------
In the olden days, the word सभा was used to indicate a big hall reserved for गम्ब्लिन्ग्. The सभापति was an officer appointed by the king to see that गम्ब्लिन्ग् was done as per the rules and collected fees or taxes from them.
If the word सभा refers to an assembly of elders and wise persons (vidvatsabhā), then the सभापति was the one who presided over such an assembly.
Sabhāpati is also one of the epithets of Lord शिव. शिव is a great master of all the 108 modes of dance. In fact, he is their creator. He is said to dance every evening in order to relieve the sufferings of creatures and entertain the gods who gather in कैलास (his abode) in full strength. Hence he is called सभापति (lord of the congregation).
Iconographically speaking, the image of सभापति is the same as that of नटराज, except that he is balancing himself on the left-leg and the poses of the two lower arms are reversed.

sabhya
(‘fit for a सभा’)
------------------------------------------
Derived from the word सभा (assembly), it means one who is fit to be present at a congregation of elders and wise persons; hence a good and wise person.
If सभा is taken to mean—in a more technical sense—a गम्ब्लिन्ग् hall, then a सभ्य is the officer in charge of it (= सभापति).
However, सभ्य is also the name of the last of the five, duly established, Vedic fires. It has to be kindled to the east of आहवनीय fire, either by attrition or from the embers of the आहवनीय fire. The hearth should be square, each side being twelve aṅgulas in length.
The origin of this सभ्य fire is rather shrouded in mystery. If सभा means a गम्ब्लिन्ग् hall (Ṛgveda 10.34.6), सभ्य is the general fire lit up to keep the place warm in winter. The same argument holds good if सभा means a big hall used as a rest-होउसे, built by a rich person.
Opinions differ as regards its establishment for Vedic rituals. Some feel it is optional while others (vide आपस्तम्ब Śrautasūtras 5.17.1) make it compulsory.

sabhā
(‘assembly’)
------------------------------------------
The earliest meaning of this word seems to be the गम्ब्लिन्ग् hall (vide Ṛgveda 10.34.6). Later on, it seems to have acquired other meanings like an assembly of learned persons as well as other persons needed to be present and presided over by the king. The word समिति was also used in the same sense.
In all probability it was not an elected body but an ad hoc one.
The word has sometimes been used to indicate an assembly of learned people, probably to discuss and decide some important issues before the king.
Sabhā can also mean an auditorium or a building meant for meetings.
